intro.carita: Uttama Carita (the third episode, chapters 5–13), of which this is the twelfth chapter of the text and the second-last of the carita. In the recitation tradition its presiding form is Mahāsarasvatī; this is the Gita Press viniyoga (printed before chapter 5), not a statement of the Purāṇa text. In the Gita Press pāṭha chapter 12 has no viniyoga of its own, only a dhyāna, of Durgā: radiant as a garland of lightning, seated on the shoulder of the lion, terrible, attended by maidens with sword and shield in hand, holding in her hands the discus, mace, sword, shield, arrows, bow, bowstring (गुणम्) and the threatening gesture (तर्जनीम्), fiery in nature, bearing the moon, three-eyed. The dhyāna is liturgy; the chapter itself names Caṇḍikā, Mahākālī, Lakṣmī and Alakṣmī, not Durgā.
intro.summary: The Devī, still before the gods who have just praised her, speaks (12.1). Whoever praises her daily with these hymns, with a collected mind, she will rid of every affliction (12.2). Those who recite the three stories — Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Mahiṣa, Śumbha and Niśumbha (12.3) — or hear her Māhātmya with devotion on the eighth, fourteenth and ninth lunar days (12.4) will know no sin, no misfortune born of sin, no poverty, no parting from those they love (12.5), and no fear of enemies, robbers, the king, weapons, fire or flood (12.6). The text is therefore to be recited and heard: it is the highest svastyayana (12.7). It quells the calamities of pestilence and the threefold portent (12.8); where it is rightly recited every day in her shrine she will never leave (12.9). It is to be recited at offerings, worship, the fire rite and festivals (12.10), and she accepts worship done with knowledge or without it (12.11). Heard at the great yearly worship of autumn, it frees a man from every trouble and gives him wealth, grain and sons (12.12–13); it makes him fearless, destroys his enemies and makes his family flourish (12.14–15). It is to be heard at rites of pacification, after evil dreams and under planetary affliction, and turns the evil dream into a good one (12.16–17); it brings peace to children seized by bālagrahas and reconciles men who have fallen apart (12.18), breaks the power of the wicked and, by its recitation alone, destroys rākṣasas, bhūtas and piśācas (12.19). The whole Māhātmya makes her present (12.20); the delight a year of offerings gives her — animals, flowers, arghya, incense, perfume, lamps, feeding of brāhmaṇas, homa, sprinklings and gifts — one hearing of this story gives her too, and, heard, it takes away sins and grants health (12.20–22). The telling of her births protects from evil beings, the story of her battles removes the fear of enemies, and the hymns of the gods, of the brahmarṣis and of Brahmā grant an auspicious mind (12.23–25). In a forest fire, among robbers or enemies, pursued by beasts, condemned by a king, in chains, in a storm at sea, in battle or in pain, the one who remembers her story is set free; beasts, robbers and enemies flee from him from afar (12.25–30). The seer resumes (12.31): Caṇḍikā vanishes as the gods watch (12.32–33); the gods take up their offices and their shares of the sacrifice again (12.33–34), and, with Śumbha and Niśumbha slain, the Daityas who are left go down to Pātāla (12.34–35). Medhas then gives King Suratha the lesson: eternal as she is, the Goddess comes forth again and again to protect the world (12.36); she deludes the universe and gives it birth, and grants knowledge when entreated and prosperity when pleased (12.37); the cosmic egg is pervaded by her as Mahākālī, who at the great time takes the form of Mahāmārī (12.38); she is dissolution, creation and preservation (12.39), Lakṣmī in good times and Alakṣmī in decline (12.40); and, praised and worshipped, she gives wealth, sons, a mind set on dharma and a good destiny (12.41).
intro.forms: The Devī, speaking in the first person through the whole phalaśruti (12.1–30): the one who destroys affliction (12.2), who abides where her text is recited (12.9, 12.20), and who accepts worship with love (12.11, 12.22). In the narrator’s voice she is the Blessed Caṇḍikā, fierce in valour (भगवती चण्डिका चण्डविक्रमा, 12.32), and the Blessed Goddess, eternal and still arising again and again (भगवती देवी … नित्या अपि पुनः पुनः सम्भूय, 12.36). Medhas’s closing verses name her powers: she who deludes the universe and brings it forth (12.37); Mahākālī, whose form at the great time is Mahāmārī, the great Death (12.38; the same word names the pestilence in 12.8); the unborn (अजा) and the eternal (सनातनी), who is creation and preservation as well as dissolution (12.39); Lakṣmī, giver of increase, and Alakṣmī, for ruin (12.40). Her ‘births’ (जन्मनाम्, 12.23) and ‘auspicious manifestations’ (उत्पत्तयः शुभाः, 12.14) are her appearances in the three stories. Mahākālī here is a name used in its own sense, not the liturgical presiding form of the first carita.
intro.significance: The chapter takes its name from its content (colophon: फलस्तुतिः). Its distinction is that the phalaśruti is spoken by the Devī herself, not by a narrator or a later editor: in her own voice she names the three stories (12.3), the days (12.4, 12.12), the occasions (12.10, 12.16) and the fruits of reciting, hearing and remembering them. It thus defines the text as a practice and lays the foundation on which the Saptaśatī is used in Śākta worship — daily pāṭha, the autumn Navarātra, rites of pacification. The narrative then closes the third story: the gods regain their offices and their shares of the sacrifice (12.33–34), and the surviving Daityas go to Pātāla (12.35), the terms the Devī sent to Śumbha in 8.26. Finally Medhas turns back to the king and restates the teaching he began with in chapter 1 — the Goddess deludes the world and gives it birth (12.37, as 1.55–56), and is eternal though she ‘arises’ (12.36, as 1.64–66) — so that the three stories stand between two statements of the same doctrine. Chapter 13 returns to Suratha and the merchant.
intro.grammar: A first-person speech of promise, and so a chapter of futures: स्तोष्यते, नाशयिष्यामि (12.2), कीर्तयिष्यन्ति (12.3), श्रोष्यन्ति (12.4), भविष्यति (12.5, 12.13), सम्भविष्यति (12.6), विमोक्ष्यामि (12.9) and the epic future प्रतीच्छिष्यामि (12.11), mostly in relative–correlative sentences (यः … तस्य, 12.2; ये … तेषाम्, 12.3–5; या … सा, 12.21–22). Gerundives command the practice (पठितव्यम्, श्रोतव्यम्, with an instrumental agent, 12.7; उच्चार्यम्, श्राव्यम्, 12.10) and optatives prescribe it or state its power (शमयेत्, 12.8; शृणुयात्, 12.16; मुच्येत, 12.29). Passives (पठ्यते, 12.9; क्रियते, 12.12, 12.22; मोह्यते, 12.37), locatives of occasion (12.4, 12.10, 12.16), locative absolutes (सुचरिते श्रुते, 12.22; तस्मिन् श्रुते, 12.24; पतत्सु शस्त्रेषु, 12.28; शुम्भे निहते, 12.34–35) and ablatives in -तः (शत्रुतः, दस्युतः, राजतः, 12.6) are frequent. Taddhita abstracts (दारिद्र्यम्, 12.5; सांनिध्यम्, 12.9; आरोग्यम्, 12.22) and agent compounds (शान्तिकारकम्, 12.18; बलहानिकरम्, 12.19; सन्निधिकारकम्, 12.20) describe the text’s effects. The learner also meets epic forms (नन्दते, 12.15; the neuter दुःस्वप्नम्, 12.17; the nominative उत्पत्तयः after श्रुत्वा, 12.14), the irregular stems पुंस् (पुमान्, 12.14; पुंसाम्, 12.15, 12.24) and नृ (नृभिः, नृणाम्), and, in the closing narrative, the imperfect अन्तरधीयत (12.33), the perfects चक्रुः and आययुः (12.34–35) and the absolutive सम्भूय (12.36).
intro.teaching: Literally, the chapter is a list of promises: recite, hear or remember this text, and sin, poverty, fear, disease, evil dreams and danger will leave you; then the Goddess vanishes, the gods return to their places, and Medhas tells the king what she is. The traditional uses of the chapter — the Navarātra pāṭha (12.4, 12.12), the recitation within every rite and the caṇḍī-homa (12.10), 12.13 recited as a sampuṭa — are the tradition’s, and the commentary presents them as such. As teaching, the chapter shifts the weight of worship from the rite to attention: she accepts what is offered in ignorance (12.11); one hearing equals a year of offerings (12.22); and in danger, where no rite can be performed, what saves is remembering (स्मरन्, 12.29). Medhas’s close joins this to the doctrine of chapter 1: the power that deludes the world is the power that gives knowledge when asked (12.37), and fortune and misfortune, creation and dissolution, are all hers (12.38–40). Reading the ‘enemies’ of 12.15 as inner passions is a modern reflection, not the verse’s literal sense.
themes: The Devī’s own phalaśruti: reciting, hearing, remembering
One hearing outweighs a year of offerings
The gods restored, the remnant in Pātāla
Eternal, yet arising again and again
Delusion and knowledge, Lakṣmī and Alakṣmī: one power

conclusion.narrative: Before she leaves, the Goddess tells the gods what the story of her deeds will do for those who keep it. Whoever praises her with these hymns, recites the three stories or hears them on the sacred days is freed from sin, poverty, fear, pestilence, evil dreams and the malice of spirits; where it is recited she is present; one hearing pleases her as much as a year of costly worship; and anyone who remembers her story in fire, flood, prison, battle or pain is set free. Then she vanishes before their eyes. The gods take back their offices and their shares of the sacrifice, and the surviving Daityas withdraw to Pātāla. Medhas gives the king the meaning of everything he has heard: the eternal Goddess comes forth again and again to protect the world; she deludes it and gives it birth, ends it, creates and sustains it; she is fortune and misfortune; and, praised and worshipped, she gives wealth, children, a mind set on dharma and a good end.

vocabulary.en: the praise of the fruits (of recitation): the chapter’s title in the colophon
greatness, glory; here the name of the text itself (12.4, 12.7, 12.14)
hymn of praise; the gods’ and others’ hymns (12.2)
a means of well-being, a rite of blessing (12.7)
presence, nearness: the Devī abiding where her text is recited (12.9; compare सन्निधिकारकम्, 12.20)
a rite of pacification, for averting harm (12.16)
delight, love: what worship and hearing give the Devī (12.11, 12.22)
remembering: the act that saves in danger (12.29; स्मरतः, 12.30)
the great pestilence (12.8); the great Death, her form at dissolution (12.38–39)
misfortune, the opposite of Lakṣmī; also her form in decline (12.40)

constructions: Promises in the future within relative–correlative sentences: यः … स्तोष्यते, तस्य … नाशयिष्यामि (12.2); two relative clauses (ये … कीर्तयिष्यन्ति, 12.3; ये … श्रोष्यन्ति, 12.4) taken up by one correlative (तेषाम्, 12.5).
Gerundives of obligation, with the agent in the instrumental (पठितव्यं समाहितैः, श्रोतव्यम्, 12.7) and a causative pair for reciting and making heard (उच्चार्यं श्राव्यम्, 12.10).
The optative of prescription and of capacity: शृणुयात् ‘one should hear’ (12.16), शमयेत् ‘would quell’ (12.8), मुच्येत ‘would be freed’ (12.29).

Locatives of occasion in series (बलिप्रदाने पूजायाम् अग्निकार्ये महोत्सवे, 12.10; शान्तिकर्मणि … दुःस्वप्नदर्शने … ग्रहपीडासु, 12.16) and locative absolutes (सकृत् सुचरिते श्रुते, 12.22; पतत्सु शस्त्रेषु, 12.28; शुम्भे निहते … निशुम्भे च, 12.34–35).
Ablatives in -तः for sources of fear (शत्रुतः, दस्युतः, राजतः, 12.6), and the ablative with a verb of fleeing (स्मरतः … पलायन्ते, 12.30).
Long sentences across verses: 12.3–5, 12.12–13, 12.20b–22a (the year of worship weighed against one hearing), and 12.25b–29a, a list of perils in apposition to नरः closed by स्मरन् … मुच्येत.
सा एव repeated in series (12.37, 12.39, 12.40) and antithesis term by term (भवकाले / अभावे, लक्ष्मीः / अलक्ष्मीः, वृद्धिप्रदा / विनाशाय, 12.40).
The genitive absolute of spectators (पश्यताम् एव देवानाम्, 12.33) and a concessive with अपि (नित्या अपि … सम्भूय, 12.36).
insights: The Goddess vouches for her own text: the phalaśruti is spoken in her voice, and its condition is attention and devotion — समाहितः, भक्त्या, एकचेतसः (12.2, 12.4, 12.7) — not learning.
Worship is accepted for love, not for correctness: she takes what is offered knowingly or unknowingly (12.11), and one hearing of her story gives her the delight of a year of offerings (12.20–22).
Remembrance is the last refuge: in fire, captivity, storm, battle and pain, where no rite is possible, the one who remembers her story is freed (12.25–30).
Manifestation is her way of protecting: eternal, she comes forth again and again (12.36), and withdraws when the work is done (12.33) — the pattern of all three stories.
One power binds and frees: she deludes the universe and gives knowledge when asked (12.37), returning to Medhas’s first teaching (1.55–57).
Nothing is outside her: dissolution, creation and preservation (12.39), Lakṣmī and Alakṣmī (12.40) are all her forms.
conclusion.srividya: The chapter shares names with the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa), noted on the verses: for the promised fruits पापनाशिनी (167) and सर्वापद्विनिवारिणी (913, 12.5), भयापहा (121, 12.6), स्वस्तिमती (448, 12.7) and सर्वव्याधिप्रशमनी (551, 12.8); for the Goddess herself चण्डिका (755) and भगवती (279, 12.32), नित्या (136, 12.36), मोहिनी (562) and वियदादिजगत्प्रसूः (550, 12.37), महाकाली (751, 12.38), and the triad सृष्टिकर्त्री (264), गोप्त्री (266), संहारिणी (268) with अजा (866, 12.39). These are shared Śākta names and ideas, not evidence that one text depends on the other. The chapter states no specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine, and its dhyāna in the Gita Press pāṭha is of Durgā, not of a Śrīvidyā form.

key_verses.why: Whoever praises me daily with these hymns, with a collected mind — every affliction of his I will destroy, without doubt.
Freed from every affliction, endowed with wealth, grain and sons, a man will be so by my grace — the line recited on its own as a sampuṭa (variant in GRETIL and Freund).
The delight a year of offerings gives me, a single hearing of this story gives too; heard, it takes away sins and grants health.
Remembering this story of mine, a man is freed from danger; by my power lions, robbers and enemies (flee, 12.30).
Though eternal, the Blessed Goddess comes forth again and again, O king, to protect the world.
By her the universe is deluded and by her it is born; entreated, she grants knowledge; pleased, prosperity.
She alone is the great Death in its time; she, the unborn, becomes creation; she, the eternal, sustains beings.

sandhi_patterns: Visarga sandhi throughout: -aḥ → -o before voiced sounds (शत्रुतो न, 12.6; नरो मुच्येत, 12.29; आघूर्णितो वा, 12.27); visarga → ś/s before c/t (स्तवैश्च, 12.2; ग्रहपीडाश्च, 12.17; कृतास्तास्तु, 12.25; वैरिणस्तथा, 12.29); visarga after other vowels → r before voiced sounds (प्रीतिर्मे, 12.22; नृभिर्दृष्टम्, 12.17; सृष्टिर्भवति, 12.39; चक्रुर्विनिहतारयः, 12.34); and visarga kept before a sibilant (रिपवः संक्षयम्, 12.15; उपसर्गाः शमम्, 12.17).

Final t → n before a nasal (तस्मान्मम, 12.7; शमयेन्मम, 12.8; शृणुयान्मम, 12.16; यन्मे, 12.23), → c before c (एतच्चरितम्, 12.10), voiced before voiced sounds (तद्वद् वधम्, 12.3; पठनादेव, 12.19; दूरादेव, 12.30); n + ś → ñch (तस्मिञ्छ्रुते, 12.24); n → ṃs/ṃś before t/c (उपसर्गानशेषांस्तु, 12.8; पुत्रांश्च, 12.41); k → ṅ before n (सम्यङ् नित्यम्, 12.9).

Pūrvarūpa with avagraha (तेऽपि, 12.33; बन्धगतोऽपि, 12.27; वेदनाभ्यर्दितोऽपि, 12.28; महोग्रेऽतुलविक्रमे, 12.35); the print also marks some savarṇa-dīrgha junctions with avagraha (जानताऽजानता, 12.11; तथाऽऽरोग्यम्, 12.22; तथाऽलक्ष्मीः, 12.40).
One declared hiatus: तुष्टा | ऋद्धिम् (12.37), required by the metre.
samasa: Dvandvas for the lists of the phalaśruti: itaretara (शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः, 12.3; रक्षोभूतपिशाचानाम्, 12.19; पशुपुष्पार्घ्यधूपैः, गन्धदीपैः, 12.20) and samāhāra (शस्त्रानलतोयौघात्, 12.6; अहर्निशम्, 12.21), and dvandvas nested in tatpuruṣas (मधुकैटभनाशम्, 12.3; धनधान्यसुतान्वितः, 12.13; सिंहव्याघ्रानुयातः, 12.26).

Tatpuruṣas with participles for the states of the hearer: tṛtīyā (भक्तिसमन्वितः, 12.12; सर्वाबाधाविनिर्मुक्तः, 12.13; दावाग्निपरिवारितः, 12.25; वेदनाभ्यर्दितः, 12.28), dvitīyā (बन्धगतः, 12.27), pañcamī (दुष्कृतोत्थाः, 12.5), caturthī (शान्तिकर्मणि, 12.16), saptamī (वह्निहोमम्, 12.11; वनहस्तिभिः, 12.26).

Agent compounds for the text’s effects and the actors: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣas in -कारक (शान्तिकारकम्, 12.18; सन्निधिकारकम्, 12.20) and upapada tatpuruṣas (बलहानिकरम्, 12.19; यज्ञभागभुजः, 12.34; जगद्विध्वंसिनि, 12.35; भूप, 12.36; वृद्धिप्रदा, 12.40).

Prādi and nañ compounds of good and ill (दुष्कृतम्, 12.5; दुःस्वप्नम्, सुस्वप्नम्, 12.17; सुचरिते, 12.22; अलक्ष्मीः, 12.40), an avyayībhāva (असंशयम्, 12.2), bahuvrīhis of state and epithet (एकचेतसः, 12.4; निर्भयः, 12.14; चण्डविक्रमा, 12.32; निरातङ्काः, 12.33; विनिहतारयः, 12.34; अतुलविक्रमे, महावीर्ये, 12.35; महामारीस्वरूपया, 12.38), and karmadhārayas of the divine names (महाकाल्या, 12.38; महामारी, 12.39).
grammar_notes: Epic (ārṣa) forms are kept and explained, not corrected: the future प्रतीच्छिष्यामि on the present stem इच्छ- (12.11), ātmanepada नन्दते (12.15), the nominative उत्पत्तयः as object of श्रुत्वा (12.14), and the neuter दुःस्वप्नम् / सुस्वप्नम् (12.17).
वार्षिकी (12.12) is read as ‘annual’ (from वर्ष ‘year’), not ‘of the rainy season’; प्रसूयते (12.37) as the active ātmanepada of the divādi root, not a passive.
स्मरतः (12.30) is read as the ablative with a verb of fleeing; a genitive is possible. महाकाले (12.38) is taken with महामारीस्वरूपया; it could go with व्याप्तम्.
The three epithets of 12.35a are taken with तस्मिन् = Śumbha, resuming 12.34; grammatically they could qualify निशुम्भे.
12.30 and 12.32 are half-ślokas (ardha) counted as mantras of their own, as the colophon count requires; the ॐ of 12.1 and 12.41 is the pāṭha’s bīja, not part of the verse.
themes: The Devī’s phalaśruti in her own voice
The restoration of the gods and the end of the third story
The eternal Goddess who arises again and again
uncertain: 12.7: स्वस्त्ययनं हि तत् (Gita Press) / स्वस्त्ययनं महत् (GRETIL, Freund) — Textual Verification Required; the sense is hardly affected.
12.13: धनधान्यसुतान्वितः (Gita Press) / धनधान्यसमन्वितः (GRETIL, Freund, without ‘sons’) — Textual Verification Required.
12.33: पश्यतामेव देवानां (Gita Press) / पश्यतां सर्वदेवानां (GRETIL, Freund) — Textual Verification Required; the sense is the same.
12.35: जगद्विध्वंसिनि (Gita Press) / जगद्विध्वंसके (GRETIL, Freund) — Textual Verification Required; the variant gives the regular anuṣṭubh cadence, the Gita Press reading a light sixth syllable.

Interpretive doubts, none about the reading itself, are flagged on 12.11 (तथा कृताम्: ‘performed thus’ or ‘likewise performed’), 12.12 (वार्षिकी), 12.14 (nominative उत्पत्तयः), 12.17 (neuter दुःस्वप्नम्), 12.21 (या as the relative of प्रीतिः in 12.22) and 12.35 (the referent of the epithets); 12.7, 12.13, 12.33 and 12.35 carry the variants above.

sandhi.note: Final ī before a dissimilar vowel becomes y: देवी + उवाच → देव्युवाच. देवी here is a singular, not a pragṛhya dual, so the vowels fuse.

morph.note: Perfect of √वच् with samprasāraṇa in the reduplication (उ-वाच); the narrative past, as in 1.1.

comm.t: The Devī answers the gods. At the end of chapter 11 she has granted them a boon and promised to return whenever demons oppress the world (11.37–55); now, still before them, she adds her own account of what the recitation of her deeds will bring. The speech runs to 12.30, after which Medhas resumes the narrative (12.31). In recitation this mantra carries the bīja ॐ, which belongs to the pāṭha, not to the verse.

mantras.anvaya: यः समाहितः (सन्) एभिः स्तवैः च मां नित्यं स्तोष्यते, तस्य सकलां बाधाम् अहम् असंशयं नाशयिष्यामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative–correlative sentence: the relative clause (यः … स्तोष्यते) describes the devotee; the main clause, with अहम् as subject, gives the promise.
mantras.lit: And whoever, with a collected mind, will constantly praise me with these hymns — every affliction of his I will destroy, without doubt.
mantras.tr: Whoever praises me daily with these hymns, with a mind at rest in me, every trouble of his I will surely destroy.
mantras.tr_note: ‘With a mind at rest in me’ renders समाहितः, ‘collected, concentrated’; the object of the concentration is implied by the context.

comm.t: The first promise of the phalaśruti. ‘These hymns’ (एभिः स्तवैः) are the praises the gods have just sung — above all the hymn of chapter 11 — and, by extension, the other hymns of the text (chapters 1, 4 and 5). The condition is twofold: regularity (नित्यम्) and attention (समाहितः).
In the Śākta tradition this verse is cited to justify the daily recitation of the hymns of the Saptaśatī on their own, apart from the whole text, when time does not allow the full pāṭha.
A modern reading: the promise is made not to the learned but to the attentive. What the verse asks for is steadiness of mind, not ritual elaboration.

mantras.anvaya: ये मधुकैटभनाशं च महिषासुरघातनं (च) तद्वत् शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः वधं (च) कीर्तयिष्यन्ति, …
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause with three objects, one for each carita; its correlative (तेषाम्) comes in 12.5, after a second relative clause in 12.4.
mantras.lit: Those who will proclaim the destruction of Madhu and Kaiṭabha and the slaying of the asura Mahiṣa, and likewise the killing of Śumbha and Niśumbha —
mantras.tr: Those who recite the destruction of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the slaying of Mahiṣāsura, and likewise the killing of Śumbha and Niśumbha —
mantras.tr_note: The sentence is completed in 12.5.

comm.t: The Devī names the three stories of the text in order: Madhu and Kaiṭabha (chapter 1), Mahiṣa (chapters 2–4), Śumbha and Niśumbha (chapters 5–10). What is to be recited is the whole narrative, not the hymns alone.

The verse is read as the Goddess’s own authority for the three-carita structure of the pāṭha. The Gita Press pāṭha assigns the three caritas to Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī as presiding forms; that is liturgical tradition, not stated here.

mantras.anvaya: ये च एव अष्टम्यां चतुर्दश्यां नवम्यां च एकचेतसः (सन्तः) भक्त्या मम उत्तमं माहात्म्यं श्रोष्यन्ति, …
mantras.anvaya_en: A second relative clause, parallel to 12.3: the first speaks of those who recite, this one of those who listen. Both are taken up by तेषाम् in 12.5.
mantras.lit: And also those who, with one-pointed minds, on the eighth, the fourteenth and the ninth (lunar days), will listen with devotion to my supreme Māhātmya —
mantras.tr: and those who, on the eighth, the fourteenth and the ninth days of the lunar fortnight, listen with devotion and undivided mind to this supreme account of my glory —
mantras.tr_note: ‘Of the lunar fortnight’ makes explicit the तिथि implied by the feminine ordinals. ‘Account of my glory’ renders माहात्म्यम्, which here names the text.

comm.t: The Devī names three lunar days (tithis) as especially fit for hearing the text: the eighth, the fourteenth and the ninth. The verse speaks of listening, as 12.3 spoke of reciting; both are then promised the same fruit in 12.5.

Aṣṭamī and navamī, above all in the bright fortnight of the autumn month Āśvina, are the climactic days of the Navarātra worship of Durgā; caturdaśī is traditionally associated with the worship of the Goddess in her fierce forms. The tradition takes these as days for the full pāṭha.

mantras.anvaya: तेषां किञ्चित् दुष्कृतं न (भविष्यति), दुष्कृतोत्थाः आपदः च न (भविष्यन्ति), दारिद्र्यं न भविष्यति, इष्टवियोजनं च एव न (भविष्यति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main clause for the relatives of 12.3–4: four negated clauses share one verb, भविष्यति, with तेषाम् as the genitive of possession (‘for them there will be no …’).
mantras.lit: For them there will be no evil deed whatever, nor misfortunes arising from evil deeds; there will be no poverty, nor indeed separation from those dear to them.
mantras.tr: For them no sin will remain, nor the misfortunes that sin brings; they will know neither poverty nor parting from those they love.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Will remain’ renders the negated भविष्यति for दुष्कृतम्, where ‘there will be no sin for them’ would be stiff; the sense is that sin will not attach to them.

comm.t: The fruit promised to those of 12.3–4 is negative: four things will not befall them — sin (दुष्कृतम्), its consequences (दुष्कृतोत्थाः आपदः), poverty, and separation from the beloved. The order moves from the moral cause to its worldly results.
The pairing of दुष्कृत with दुष्कृतोत्थाः आपदः is read in the light of the doctrine of karma: the recitation is said to remove not only present misfortunes but their root in past deeds.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess पापनाशिनी (name 167) and सर्वापद्विनिवारिणी (name 913), ‘destroyer of sin’ and ‘warder-off of all misfortunes’: the same two promises as this verse, made in a separate work.

samasa.literal: from weapon, fire and flood of water
samasa.sense: from any of the three dangers: weapons, fire, floods
samasa.alt: Also readable as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa over a dvandva, शस्त्रानलतोयानाम् ओघः, ‘an onrush of weapons, fire and water’; the singular ending fits either. The dvandva gives three distinct dangers, as the verse lists distinct sources of fear.

morph.note: The taddhita affix तसिल् (-तः) forms indeclinables with the sense of the ablative: शत्रुतः = शत्रोः ‘from an enemy’. Likewise दस्युतः and राजतः (राजन् loses its n before the affix).
Future of सम् + √भू, ‘will come about, will arise’; one verb for every clause of the verse.

mantras.anvaya: तस्य शत्रुतः भयं न (सम्भविष्यति), दस्युतः वा न, राजतः न, शस्त्रानलतोयौघात् (च भयं) कदाचित् न सम्भविष्यति।
mantras.anvaya_en: One subject (भयम्), one verb (सम्भविष्यति, given at the end), and four negated sources of fear in the ablative, three of them indeclinables in -तः.
mantras.lit: For him there will be no fear from enemies, or from robbers, nor from the king; nor will (fear) ever arise from weapons, fire or floods of water.
mantras.tr: He need never fear enemies, robbers or the king, nor weapons, fire or flood.
mantras.tr_note: The future ‘there will be no fear’ is rendered as ‘he need never fear’; कदाचित् with न (‘never’) is taken with the whole verse.

comm.t: A second list of promises, of dangers from outside: enemies, robbers, the king’s anger, weapons, fire, water. The subject moves from the plural तेषाम् of 12.5 to the generic singular तस्य, ‘(any) such person’.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) calls the Goddess भयापहा (name 121), ‘remover of fear’ — the title this verse spells out danger by danger.
A modern reading: the list is the list of an ancient household’s real fears — war, theft, the arbitrary ruler, fire, flood. The promise answers the insecurity of ordinary life, not only of the soul.

mantras.anvaya: तस्मात् मम एतत् माहात्म्यं समाहितैः सदा भक्त्या पठितव्यं श्रोतव्यं च; तत् हि परं स्वस्त्ययनम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A command expressed by two gerundives in the passive construction (agent समाहितैः in the instrumental), followed by a nominal clause with हि giving the reason.
mantras.lit: Therefore this Māhātmya of mine is to be recited by those of collected mind, and always to be heard with devotion; for it is the supreme means of well-being.
mantras.tr: So let this account of my glory be recited with a gathered mind and always heard with devotion; for it is the highest blessing.
mantras.tr_note: The gerundives (‘is to be recited’) are rendered as exhortations (‘let … be recited’). ‘The highest blessing’ condenses परं स्वस्त्ययनम्, ‘the supreme means of welfare’.

comm.t: The conclusion of the first group of promises: because of all this (तस्मात्), the text is to be recited and heard, with attention and with devotion. The reason given is that it is a स्वस्त्ययन, a rite of blessing.

स्वस्त्ययन is a technical word for the protective and auspicious rites of the household; by calling her own Māhātmya the ‘highest svastyayana’, the Devī places its recitation among such rites — which is how the tradition uses it.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name स्वस्तिमती (name 448), ‘she who is possessed of well-being (svasti)’ — the same word for welfare that forms स्वस्त्ययन here.

morph.note: Optative of the causative of √शम् (शमय- with the short a that this root keeps in the causative). The optative states what the text is able to do: ‘would quell, can quell’.

mantras.anvaya: मम माहात्म्यं महामारीसमुद्भवान् अशेषान् उपसर्गान् तथा त्रिविधम् उत्पातं तु शमयेत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A simple active sentence: subject माहात्म्यम्, verb शमयेत्, two objects (उपसर्गान् and उत्पातम्) joined by तथा.
mantras.lit: My Māhātmya would quell all calamities arising from the great pestilence, and likewise the threefold portent.
mantras.tr: My Māhātmya stills every affliction that pestilence brings, and the three kinds of evil omen.
mantras.tr_note: The optative शमयेत् (‘would quell’) is rendered as a present of capacity.

comm.t: The recitation is said to quell two kinds of danger that no human action can avert: epidemic disease and portents. महामारी, the great pestilence, will later be named as a form of the Devī herself (12.38–39), who is both the plague and its cure.

Portents (उत्पात) are traditionally divided into three kinds — the heavenly (दिव्य), the atmospheric (आन्तरिक्ष) and the earthly (भौम) — and त्रिविधम् is usually explained in this way. Recitation of the Saptaśatī as a rite of śānti in times of epidemic rests on this verse.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess सर्वव्याधिप्रशमनी (name 551), ‘she who allays all disease’, using the same verb (प्र + √शम्) as शमयेत् here.

mantras.anvaya: यत्र मम आयतने एतत् नित्यं सम्यक् पठ्यते, तत् (अहं) सदा न विमोक्ष्यामि; तत्र मे सांनिध्यं स्थितम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause of place (यत्र …) and two main clauses: a verbal one in the first person (न विमोक्ष्यामि with object तत्) and a nominal one (सांनिध्यं … स्थितम्) introduced by the correlative तत्र.
mantras.lit: In whatever shrine of mine this is properly recited daily, that (place) I will never abandon; my presence is established there.
mantras.tr: Wherever in my shrine this is rightly recited every day, that place I will never leave: there my presence abides.

comm.t: The Devī promises her permanent presence (सांनिध्य) wherever the text is recited correctly and regularly. The condition is again twofold, as in 12.2: correctness (सम्यक्) and regularity (नित्यम्).

आयतन means a temple or sanctuary, but also any dwelling; the tradition applies the verse to the household shrine as well as the temple, and understands the daily pāṭha as making the place a seat of the Goddess.
A modern reading: the promise is attached to a practice, not to a building. Presence is said to follow faithful, regular attention, wherever it is given.

morph.note: उद् + √चर्, causative उच्चारय- ‘to make go up, to utter’; with ण्यत् (-य) and loss of the causative suffix: उच्चार्य ‘to be uttered aloud’. The d of उद् is assimilated to c (उच्चर्).
From the causative श्रावय- of √श्रु: ‘to be caused to be heard’, i.e. to be recited for others to hear. The pair उच्चार्यं श्राव्यं covers reciting oneself and having it heard.

mantras.anvaya: बलिप्रदाने पूजायाम् अग्निकार्ये महोत्सवे (च) मम एतत् सर्वं चरितम् उच्चार्यं श्राव्यं च एव।
mantras.anvaya_en: Four locatives of occasion, then a subject (चरितम्) with two gerundives as predicate.
mantras.lit: At the presenting of offerings, at worship, at the fire rite, at a great festival — this entire story of my deeds is to be recited aloud and indeed to be made heard.
mantras.tr: At every offering, at worship, at the fire rite and at great festivals, this whole story of my deeds should be recited and heard.
mantras.tr_note: श्राव्यम् strictly means ‘to be made heard’ (recited for others); ‘heard’ keeps the line simple.

comm.t: The Devī names the occasions at which her whole story (सर्वं चरितम्) should be recited: the giving of bali, worship, the fire rite and great festivals. The emphasis on सर्वम् asks for the complete text, not excerpts.
The tradition reads the verse as the basis for reciting the Saptaśatī within every major Śākta rite, and for the homa in which its mantras are offered into the fire (the caṇḍī-homa).

Instrumental of the present participle जानत् (√ज्ञा, kryādi, present stem जानी-/जान-). With the past participle कृताम् the doer stands in the instrumental: ‘done by one who knows’.

mantras.anvaya: जानता अजानता वा अपि तथा कृतां बलिपूजां तथा कृतं वह्निहोमं (च) अहं प्रीत्या प्रतीच्छिष्यामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject अहम्, verb प्रतीच्छिष्यामि, two objects each with a participle कृत; the instrumentals जानता / अजानता give the doer of both.
mantras.lit: Worship with offerings so performed, by one who knows or even by one who does not know, I will accept with love; and the fire oblation likewise performed.
mantras.tr: Whether the worship and offerings are made with knowledge or without it, I will accept them gladly, and the fire oblation too.
mantras.tr_note: तथा कृताम् is taken as ‘performed thus’, i.e. together with the recitation just prescribed in 12.10; the translation folds this into the sentence.

comm.t: Continuing 12.10: when the worship and the homa are accompanied by the recitation, the Devī accepts them with love whether the worshipper knows the correct procedure or not. Knowledge of ritual detail is not the condition of acceptance.
The tradition reads this as a promise that the recitation of the Saptaśatī makes good the defects of ritual performed in ignorance — which is why it is recited alongside other rites.
A modern reading: the Goddess here is no exacting examiner. Sincerity — the प्रीति that answers devotion — matters more than technical perfection.

flags.uncertain: तथा कृताम् / तथा कृतम्: तथा may mean ‘performed in that way’ (with the recitation of 12.10) or simply ‘likewise performed’; the first is followed. The future प्रतीच्छिष्यामि is non-classical (see Morph).

वार्षिक, a taddhita derivative of वर्ष with vṛddhi of the first syllable and the affix -इक; feminine in -ई. It can mean ‘yearly’ (from वर्ष ‘year’) or ‘of the rains’ (from वर्षा).
Absolutive of √श्रु with क्त्वा; its subject is the person of 12.13 (मनुष्यः), whose main verb is भविष्यति.

mantras.anvaya: शरत्काले या च वार्षिकी महापूजा क्रियते, तस्यां मम एतत् माहात्म्यं श्रुत्वा भक्तिसमन्वितः (मनुष्यः) …
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या … क्रियते) names the occasion; तस्याम् resumes it. The participial phrase ending in भक्तिसमन्वितः describes the subject of 12.13.
mantras.lit: And at the great worship which is performed in autumn, the annual one — at that, having heard this Māhātmya of mine, (a man) full of devotion …
mantras.tr: At the great yearly worship held in autumn, the one who hears this account of my glory with devotion
mantras.tr_note: The sentence continues into 12.13.

comm.t: The Devī singles out the great annual worship in autumn. Hearing the text then, with devotion, brings the fruits listed in the next verse.

This verse is the classic textual warrant for the Śāradīya Navarātra (Durgā Pūjā), the autumn festival in which the Saptaśatī is recited over nine nights; the aṣṭamī and navamī of 12.4 are its central days.

flags.uncertain: वार्षिकी is taken as ‘annual’ (from वर्ष ‘year’). It could also mean ‘belonging to the rainy season’ (from वर्षा); the tradition, which identifies the rite with the autumn Navarātra, follows ‘annual’.

mantras.anvaya_en: The main clause of the sentence begun in 12.12: subject मनुष्यः, verb भविष्यति, two predicate adjectives; then a short verbless clause, न संशयः.
mantras.lit: … a man, by my grace, will become freed from all afflictions and endowed with wealth, grain and sons; there is no doubt.
mantras.tr: will by my grace be freed from every trouble and blessed with wealth, grain and children. Of this there is no doubt.
mantras.tr_note: सुत (‘sons’) is rendered ‘children’ in the readable translation; the literal translation keeps ‘sons’.

comm.t: Completing 12.12: the devotee who hears the text at the autumn worship is freed from afflictions and prospers in wealth, grain and offspring — and the Devī adds her own guarantee, न संशयः.

The verse is among the best-known lines of the Saptaśatī and is widely recited on its own as a mantra for well-being and prosperity, for example as a sampuṭa (a line enclosing each verse) in a pāṭha undertaken for a particular wish. That use belongs to the later ritual tradition, not to the Purāṇa.
A modern reading: the blessing is concrete — freedom from trouble, food, family — and it is said to come ‘by my grace’ (मत्प्रसादेन), not as the automatic wage of a rite.

Nominative singular of the irregular stem पुंस् ‘man’ (strong stem पुमांस्-); genitive plural पुंसाम् in 12.15.

mantras.anvaya: मम एतत् माहात्म्यं तथा च (मम) शुभाः उत्पत्तयः युद्धेषु (मम) पराक्रमं च श्रुत्वा पुमान् निर्भयः जायते।
mantras.anvaya_en: An absolutive with three objects (माहात्म्यम्, उत्पत्तयः, पराक्रमम्) and a main clause with subject पुमान्, verb जायते and predicate निर्भयः.
mantras.lit: Having heard this Māhātmya of mine, and likewise the auspicious manifestations, and (my) valour in battles, a man becomes fearless.
mantras.tr: One who hears this account of my glory — my auspicious manifestations and my valour in battle — becomes free of fear.
mantras.tr_note: The readable translation takes the manifestations and the valour as the content of the Māhātmya, which is what the text is; the Sanskrit lists them side by side with तथा च.

comm.t: Three things heard — the Māhātmya, the Devī’s auspicious manifestations (उत्पत्तयः) and her valour in battle — make the hearer fearless. The manifestations are her appearances in the text: from the gods’ tejas (chapter 2), from the body of Pārvatī (chapter 5), and the forms foretold in 11.41–55.
The tradition connects the fruit with the content: one who has heard how the Goddess overcame every enemy in battle shares in her fearlessness.

flags.uncertain: उत्पत्तयः शुभाः is nominative where the accusative is expected after श्रुत्वा; it is construed as a second object (an ārṣa looseness). The Gita Press reading is kept.

mantras.anvaya: मम माहात्म्यं शृण्वतां पुंसां रिपवः संक्षयं यान्ति, कल्याणं च उपपद्यते, कुलं च नन्दते।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three coordinate clauses with different subjects (रिपवः, कल्याणम्, कुलम्); the genitive phrase पुंसां … शृण्वताम् (‘of men who hear’) belongs to all three.
mantras.lit: Enemies go to destruction, welfare comes about, and the family rejoices — of men who hear my Māhātmya.
mantras.tr: For those who hear my glory, enemies perish, good fortune comes, and their family flourishes.
mantras.tr_note: The genitive पुंसां शृण्वताम् is grammatically attached to कुलम्; the readable translation lets it govern all three clauses, as the sense requires.

comm.t: Three further fruits for those who hear the text: the destruction of enemies, the arrival of welfare, and the flourishing of the family.

A modern reading may take the ‘enemies’ (रिपवः) inwardly as well, as the passions Indian thought calls the six inner enemies (षड्रिपु). The verse itself speaks of outward enemies, beside welfare and family.

samasa.sense: after an ill-omened dream
troubles attributed to unfavourable planets
samasa.alt: Also readable as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, ग्रहाणां पीडाः ‘the planets’ afflictions’; the sense is the same.

morph.note: Optative of √श्रु (stem शृणु- + याः + त्): ‘one should hear’ — the optative of prescription.
Locative singular of the n-stem कर्मन् (कर्मणि, with ṇ after r).

mantras.anvaya: सर्वत्र शान्तिकर्मणि तथा दुःस्वप्नदर्शने उग्रासु ग्रहपीडासु च मम माहात्म्यं शृणुयात्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three locatives of occasion and one prescriptive optative, with an unexpressed generic subject (‘one’).
mantras.lit: In every rite of pacification, likewise on seeing a bad dream, and in severe afflictions from the planets, one should hear my Māhātmya.
mantras.tr: At every rite for averting harm, after an evil dream, and when the planets afflict severely, let my glory be heard.
mantras.tr_note: The optative ‘one should hear’ is rendered as an impersonal ‘let … be heard’.

comm.t: The Devī prescribes her Māhātmya for three occasions of śānti (averting harm): propitiatory rites in general, bad dreams, and planetary afflictions. The next verse gives the result for each.
On this verse the tradition prescribes the Saptaśatī pāṭha as a remedy in the rites of pacification connected with dreams and planets, in place of or alongside other propitiatory rites.

an ominous dream
an auspicious dream

morph.note: उप + √जन्, present: ‘arises, comes to be’; with the predicate सुस्वप्नम् it means ‘turns into a good dream’.
Instrumental plural of the r-stem नृ ‘man’ (नृ + भिस्); agent of the participle दृष्टम्.
स्वप्न is masculine; the neuter here (with दृष्टम्, सुस्वप्नम्) treats ‘a bad dream’ as a thing seen. Epic usage allows this; the meaning is unaffected.

mantras.anvaya: उपसर्गाः दारुणाः ग्रहपीडाः च शमं यान्ति; नृभिः दृष्टं दुःस्वप्नं च सुस्वप्नम् उपजायते।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: the first with two subjects and the idiom शमं यान्ति ‘come to rest’; the second with subject दुःस्वप्नम्, verb उपजायते and the predicate सुस्वप्नम्.
mantras.lit: Calamities go to rest, and the dreadful afflictions from the planets; and a bad dream seen by men becomes a good dream.
mantras.tr: Calamities are stilled, and the harsh afflictions of the planets; and the evil dream that men have seen turns into a good one.

comm.t: The result of the hearing prescribed in 12.16: calamities and planetary afflictions subside, and an evil dream is turned into a good one — its bad omen is reversed.
A modern reading: what was dreaded does not merely disappear; it is changed into its opposite. Fear met with the remembrance of grace can become a sign of protection.

flags.uncertain: दुःस्वप्नम् / सुस्वप्नम् are neuter here though स्वप्न is normally masculine; the forms are taken as epic usage, not as a corruption.

that which brings relief, pacifies

samasa.literal: in the breaking of a union
samasa.sense: when people bound together fall apart
a means of reconciliation

morph.note: कारक is √कृ + ण्वुल् (-अक), an agent noun ‘maker’; neuter here to agree with the understood subject माहात्म्यम्.
Genitive plural of the r-stem नृ, with the long ṝ optional in this form; the Gita Press has नृणाम्, with ṇ after ṛ.

mantras.anvaya: (एतत् माहात्म्यं) बालग्रहाभिभूतानां बालानां शान्तिकारकम्, नृणां संघातभेदे च उत्तमं मैत्रीकरणम् (भवति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two nominal predicates of an unexpressed subject, the Māhātmya (named in 12.16): ‘(it is) a bringer of peace … and the best means of friendship …’.
mantras.lit: (It is) the bringer of relief for children overpowered by child-seizers, and, when a union among men is broken, the best means of making friendship.
mantras.tr: It brings peace to children seized by evil spirits, and when men who were bound together fall apart, it is the best way to make them friends again.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Evil spirits’ renders बालग्रह, a class of beings believed to afflict children; the subject ‘it’ (the Māhātmya) is supplied.

comm.t: Two further uses of the text: for children afflicted by bālagrahas, and for reconciling men whose union has broken. The subject, the Māhātmya, is carried over from the previous verses.

बालग्रह, ‘seizers of children’, are a class of beings named in the medical and Purāṇic literature as the cause of children’s illnesses; rites of protection against them were part of household religion, and the Devī here offers her Māhātmya as such a rite.

samasa.sense: of every kind of malevolent being

morph.note: कर is √कृ + ट (-अ), an agent suffix that occurs only at the end of a compound (upapada): ‘-maker’.
Ablative of the action noun पठन ‘reading, recitation’: ‘from the reading alone’ — एव restricts the cause to the recitation itself.
Action noun in -अन from the causative stem नाशय- of √नश्, used as an agent: ‘destroyer’.

mantras.anvaya: (एतत् माहात्म्यम्) अशेषाणां दुर्वृत्तानां परं बलहानिकरम्, पठनात् एव रक्षोभूतपिशाचानां नाशनम् (भवति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: As in 12.18, two nominal predicates of the unexpressed subject माहात्म्यम्.
mantras.lit: (It is) supremely the destroyer of the strength of all the wicked; by its mere reading, the destroyer of rākṣasas, bhūtas and piśācas.
mantras.tr: It utterly breaks the power of all evil-doers, and by its recitation alone it destroys demons, ghosts and goblins.
mantras.tr_note: रक्षस्, भूत and पिशाच are classes of malevolent beings; ‘demons, ghosts and goblins’ is an approximation.

comm.t: The recitation is said to break the power of evil-doers and, by the mere act of reading (पठनादेव), to destroy three classes of malevolent beings: rākṣasas, bhūtas and piśācas.
A modern reading: the verse moves from human wrongdoers to unseen terrors. In both cases the protection named is the same — the remembered story of the Goddess’s victory.

samasa.literal: with animals, flowers, arghya-waters and incense
samasa.sense: the offerings of a full worship
with sandal paste and lamps offered in worship

morph.note: कारक (√कृ + ण्वुल्) ‘maker’ as the last member of a compound; the second मम is its logical object: ‘causing my presence’.
A dvandva takes the gender of its last member (धूप, m.): masculine instrumental plural.

mantras.anvaya: मम एतत् सर्वं माहात्म्यं मम सन्निधिकारकम् (अस्ति)। पशुपुष्पार्घ्यधूपैः च तथा उत्तमैः गन्धदीपैः …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is a complete nominal sentence. The second line opens a new sentence, whose instrumentals continue through 12.21 to the main clause in 12.22 (प्रीतिः मे क्रियते …).
mantras.lit: This entire Māhātmya of mine brings about my presence. With animals, flowers, water-offerings and incense, and likewise with excellent perfumes and lamps —
mantras.tr: This whole account of my glory makes me present. With offerings of animals, flowers, water and incense, with the finest perfumes and lamps —
mantras.tr_note: The second line begins a sentence completed in 12.22 (‘the delight that is given me … by a year of worship is given me by a single hearing’).

comm.t: The first line restates 12.9: the whole Māhātmya makes the Devī present. The second line begins the list of a year’s worship — animal offerings (पशु), flowers, arghya, incense, perfumes, lamps — that will be weighed against one hearing of the text in 12.22.

The items named are the standard offerings of Purāṇic worship (upacāras). The mention of पशु reflects the animal offering of the Purāṇic rite; many Śākta communities offer a substitute instead, a practice the verse itself does not discuss.

mantras.anvaya: (पशुपुष्पार्घ्यधूपैः …) विप्राणां भोजनैः होमैः अहर्निशं प्रोक्षणीयैः अन्यैः च विविधैः भोगैः प्रदानैः (च) वत्सरेण या (प्रीतिः मे क्रियते) …
mantras.anvaya_en: A continuation of the list of instrumentals begun in 12.20; the relative या opens the clause that 12.22 completes (या प्रीतिः मे क्रियते, सा …).
mantras.lit: with feedings of brāhmaṇas, with fire oblations, with sprinklings day and night, and with various other enjoyments and gifts — the (delight) which, in a year, …
mantras.tr: with the feeding of brāhmaṇas, with oblations and lustrations day and night, with every other kind of offering and gift — the delight these give me in a whole year
mantras.tr_note: ‘The delight … give me’ anticipates प्रीतिः मे क्रियते of 12.22, to which the relative या points; the sentence is completed there.

comm.t: The list of a year’s worship continues: feeding brāhmaṇas, homa, sprinkling with consecrated water day and night, other offerings and gifts. The relative या, ‘which’, prepares the comparison of 12.22: all this, over a year, pleases the Devī no more than a single hearing of her story.
A modern reading: the long catalogue of 12.20–21 is built up only to be outweighed. The rhetorical point is the value of attentive hearing, set against an entire year of costly ritual.

flags.uncertain: The analysis of या depends on 12.22 (प्रीतिर्मे क्रियते सास्मिन्), outside this batch: या is taken as the relative of प्रीतिः, with सा as correlative.

The past participle used as a noun: ‘what has been heard’, i.e. the story once it is heard. The same participle stands just before in the locative absolute (सुचरिते श्रुते); the repetition श्रुते | श्रुतम् links the two halves.
Taddhita abstract (ṣyañ) from अरोग ‘free of disease’: अरोगस्य भावः, with vṛddhi of the first vowel (a → ā).
The present stem यच्छ- is a substitute: Pāṇini teaches यच्छ for दाण् ‘to give’ in the present system. With प्र it means ‘to hand over, bestow’.

mantras.anvaya: (… वत्सरेण या) प्रीतिः मे क्रियते, सा अस्मिन् सुचरिते सकृत् श्रुते (क्रियते)। श्रुतम् (एतत्) पापानि हरति, तथा आरोग्यं प्रयच्छति।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line closes the relative sentence of 12.20–21: ‘the satisfaction (या प्रीतिः) that is produced in me by a year of offerings — that (सा) is produced when this story is heard once’; क्रियते is understood again with सा. The second line is a new sentence with श्रुतम् as subject and two verbs.
mantras.lit: (The) satisfaction (that) is produced in me (by a year of such offerings) — that (is produced) when this good story is heard once. Heard, it takes away sins and likewise grants health.
mantras.tr: The delight that a whole year of such worship gives me, a single hearing of this holy story gives me too. Heard, it takes away sins and grants health.
mantras.tr_note: ‘A whole year of such worship’ gathers the list of 12.20–21 (वत्सरेण, ‘over a year’) which the relative या there points to. ‘Gives me too’ renders the correlative सा with क्रियते understood.

comm.t: The Devī completes the comparison begun in 12.20: animal offerings, flowers, arghya, incense, perfume, lamps, the feeding of brāhmaṇas, homa, sprinklings, and gifts kept up for a year please her no more than one hearing (सकृत्) of this story. The second line adds two further fruits of hearing: sins removed, health granted.

The recitation tradition draws from verses like this its high estimate of the pāṭha itself: hearing or reciting the text is counted as worship in its own right, not as an accompaniment to ritual. The verse does not dismiss the offerings; it measures the hearing by them.
A modern reading: the verse sets a year of outward effort beside one moment of attentive listening and finds them equal. What it values is the attention, not the quantity.

samasa.sense: the battles of chapters 2–10, named by what they achieved

mantras.anvaya: मम जन्मनां कीर्तनं भूतेभ्यः रक्षां करोति। युद्धेषु मे यत् दुष्टदैत्यनिबर्हणं चरितम्, (तस्मिन् श्रुते … 12.24)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is complete. The second opens a relative clause (यत् … चरितम्) whose main clause is 12.24a (तस्मिन् श्रुते …).
mantras.lit: The recital of my births makes protection from (evil) beings. My deed in battles, which (is) the destruction of the wicked Daityas —
mantras.tr: The telling of my births guards against evil spirits. And the story of my battles, in which the wicked Daityas were destroyed —
mantras.tr_note: भूत is rendered ‘evil spirits’ following 12.19 (रक्षोभूतपिशाचानां), where the same word stands among demons and ghouls.

comm.t: Two kinds of telling are distinguished: the recital of the Devī’s births (जन्मनाम्) and the story of her battles. Her births are the appearances told in the three caritas and the future ones she has just foretold in 11.41–55 (Vindhyavāsinī, Raktadantikā, Śatākṣī, Śākambharī, Durgā, Bhīmā, Bhrāmarī).
The tradition hears ‘births’ (जन्मन्) as manifestations: the Goddess is not born as beings are, which is why Medhas calls her eternal even as she ‘arises’ (1.64–66, and again in 12.36).

Instrumental plural of the second-person pronoun: ‘by you’. The Devī is addressing the gods.

mantras.anvaya: तस्मिन् श्रुते पुंसां वैरिकृतं भयं न जायते। याः च स्तुतयः युष्माभिः (कृताः), याः च ब्रह्मर्षिभिः कृताः, (याः च ब्रह्मणा कृताः, ताः शुभां मतिं प्रयच्छन्ति — 12.25)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line answers the relative clause of 12.23 (यत् … तस्मिन्). The second opens a new relative sentence (याः च … याः च …) that continues into 12.25 and closes with ताः.
mantras.lit: When that is heard, fear caused by enemies does not arise for men. And the hymns which (were made) by you, and which were made by the brahmin seers —
mantras.tr: When it is heard, no fear of enemies arises in anyone. And the hymns that you have sung, and those composed by the great seers,

comm.t: The story of the battles frees its hearers from fear of enemies. The Devī then turns to the hymns: those of the gods she is speaking to (युष्माभिः — the hymns of chapters 4, 5 and 11), those of the brahmarṣis, and, in the next verse, Brahmā’s (the hymn of chapter 1). The text does not say which hymns of the brahmarṣis it means.

The verse is taken to include the hymns within the Saptaśatī among the things whose recitation the Devī herself commends, so that the stutis are recited as part of the pāṭha, not as optional additions.

mantras.anvaya: (याः च) ब्रह्मणा कृताः, ताः तु शुभां मतिं प्रयच्छन्ति। अरण्ये प्रान्तरे वा अपि दावाग्निपरिवारितः (नरः … 12.29)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line closes the relative sentence opened in 12.24 with its correlative ताः. The second line begins one long sentence, a list of perils in apposition to नरः, whose verb is मुच्येत in 12.29.
mantras.lit: and (those which were) made by Brahmā — they indeed grant an auspicious mind. In a forest, or even on a lonely road, surrounded by a forest fire,
mantras.tr: and the hymn of Brahmā — these grant a mind turned to the good. In a forest or on a lonely road, ringed by a forest fire,

comm.t: The fruit of the hymns is named precisely: not wealth or safety but शुभा मतिः, a good and auspicious understanding. The second line opens the list of dangers (12.25b–28) that ends with the promise of 12.29: whoever remembers the story in any of them is freed.

Brahmā’s hymn is the one of chapter 1 (the hymn that wakes Viṣṇu), which the Śākta tradition reveres in its own right. The perils that follow are the classical list of saṅkaṭas — fire, robbers, wild beasts, a king’s anger, the sea, battle and pain — for which the text is recited.

mantras.tr: beset by robbers in some lonely place, or captured by enemies, hunted by lions and tigers, or by wild elephants in the forest,

comm.t: The list of perils continues with dangers from men (robbers, enemies) and from beasts (lions, tigers, wild elephants). The participle governing the elephants is carried over from the compound सिंहव्याघ्रानुयातः.
A modern reading: the dangers are those of a traveller far from help — the lonely place, the forest — exactly where no human protector can be summoned and only remembrance is left.

mantras.anvaya_en: More phrases in apposition to नरः (12.29): a king’s sentence, prison, and a storm at sea.
mantras.lit: or ordered by an angry king (as one) to be killed, or even gone into bonds; or tossed about by the wind while standing in a ship on the great ocean,
mantras.tr: condemned to death by an angry king, or lying in chains; or tossed by the gale on a ship on the great ocean,

comm.t: Three more perils: a death sentence from an angry king, imprisonment, and a ship caught in a storm. The order runs from danger at the hands of authority to danger from nature.
The frame gives this list a living example: Suratha, who hears these words, has lost his kingdom to enemies and his own ministers (1.5–9). The perils are not abstract for him.

mantras.anvaya: भृशदारुणे संग्रामे शस्त्रेषु पतत्सु च अपि, घोरासु सर्वाबाधासु (वा), वेदनाभ्यर्दितः अपि वा … (नरः — 12.29)
mantras.anvaya_en: A locative absolute (शस्त्रेषु पतत्सु) with its setting (संग्रामे), a locative of circumstance (सर्वाबाधासु), and a last participle in apposition to नरः.
mantras.lit: and even when weapons are falling in an exceedingly terrible battle, in all terrible afflictions, or even tormented by pain,
mantras.tr: when weapons rain down in a fearful battle, in every dire calamity, or racked with pain —

comm.t: The list closes with battle, with every kind of calamity, and with bodily pain. सर्वाबाधासु widens it to anything not yet named, echoing the gods’ request for ‘the calming of all afflictions’ (सर्वाबाधाप्रशमनं, 11.39) and the Devī’s promise in 12.13.
A modern reading: the last item is the most private — pain, where no enemy is involved at all. The promise reaches from the battlefield to the sickbed.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line gives the main clause for the whole list of 12.25b–28: the man in any of those perils, remembering the story, is freed. The second opens a new sentence whose verb is पलायन्ते in 12.30.
mantras.lit: Remembering this story of mine, a man would be freed from danger. Through my power, lions and the rest, robbers, and likewise enemies
mantras.tr: whoever remembers this story of mine is set free from peril. By my power, lions and other wild beasts, robbers and enemies
mantras.tr_note: The optative मुच्येत is rendered as a plain present (‘is set free’): it states what happens, not a wish.

comm.t: The long sentence begun in 12.25 reaches its verb: the person in any of the dangers listed, remembering (स्मरन्) the Devī’s story, is freed. स्मरन् governs the whole list: in every peril named, what saves is remembering.
The Śākta tradition sets this verse beside the Devī’s promise in 11.54–55 (‘whenever trouble arises … I shall descend’): the remembered story is how she comes to the one in trouble.
A modern reading: the verse says ‘remembering’, not ‘reciting’. In a burning forest or a storm at sea no book or ritual is to hand; what one carries inside is what is left.

comm.t: The half-verse that ends the Devī’s speech, begun at 12.2. Beasts, robbers and enemies do not merely fail to harm the one who remembers her story: they flee from far off (दूरात् एव), before any encounter.
The Gita Press pāṭha counts this half-śloka as a mantra of its own (an ardha), as the chapter colophon’s count requires. With it the Devī’s phalaśruti, spoken in her own voice, is complete.

comm.t: The half-verse that closes the Devī’s speech in the narrator’s voice and opens her disappearance. The pairing चण्डिका चण्डविक्रमा repeats the root of her name: she is caṇḍa, fierce, in name and in deed.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also has the name Caṇḍikā (name 755, चण्डिका) and Bhagavatī (name 279, भगवती). The two texts are distinct works that share a vocabulary of names.

mantras.anvaya: (सा भगवती चण्डिका) देवानां पश्यताम् एव तत्र एव अन्तरधीयत। ते अपि देवाः निरातङ्काः (सन्तः) यथा पुरा स्वाधिकारान् (12.34: … चक्रुः)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line gives the verb for the subject of 12.32. The second begins a new sentence whose verb, चक्रुः, comes in 12.34.
mantras.lit: vanished right there, even as the gods were looking on. Those gods too, free from dread, (exercised) their own offices as before —
mantras.tr: vanished then and there before the very eyes of the gods. And the gods, their dread gone, took up their own offices as of old,

comm.t: The Goddess disappears in the place where she appeared (तत्र एव), while the gods watch. The gods return to their own functions (स्वाधिकारान्), which Śumbha and Niśumbha had taken from them at the start of the third story (5.2–4). The war ends where it began.
The disappearance (अन्तरधीयत) is read as the counterpart of her ‘arising’ (उत्पन्ना, 1.66): she is not destroyed or removed, she withdraws, and comes forth again when called (12.36).
Variant: GRETIL and Freund read पश्यतां सर्वदेवानां (‘while all the gods looked on’) for the Gita Press पश्यतामेव देवानां. The sense is the same; the Gita Press reading is kept.

mantras.anvaya: सर्वे (ते देवाः) विनिहतारयः यज्ञभागभुजः (सन्तः) यथा पुरा स्वाधिकारान् चक्रुः। देव्या युधि देवरिपौ शुम्भे निहते, … (12.35) … दैत्याः च शेषाः पातालम् आययुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line finishes the sentence of 12.33b with its verb चक्रुः. The second line begins a new sentence: its subject दैत्याः, a chain of locative absolutes (शुम्भे निहते … निशुम्भे च …), and the verb आययुः in 12.35.
mantras.lit: all of them, enjoyers of sacrificial shares, their enemies slain, did (their offices). And the Daityas — Śumbha, the enemy of the gods, having been slain in battle by the Devī,
mantras.tr: all of them, their enemies destroyed, once more receiving their portions of the sacrifice. And when Śumbha, the gods’ enemy, had been slain by the Devī in battle,
mantras.tr_note: चक्रुः, ‘did’, has स्वाधिकारान् (12.33) as its object: ‘carried out their own offices’, rendered ‘took up their own offices’ in 12.33.

comm.t: The cosmic order is restored: each god holds his office again and receives his share of the sacrifice (यज्ञभाग), the right Śumbha had seized (5.2) and boasted of (5.108). The second line turns to the defeated: the Daityas, whose fate is told in 12.35.

The verse fulfils, almost word for word, the terms the Devī sent to Śumbha through Śiva as her messenger (8.26): ‘let Indra regain the three worlds, let the gods enjoy the oblations (हविर्भुजः); you go to Pātāla if you wish to live.’ The return of the sacrificial shares is the sign, in Purāṇic thought, that the world is in order again.

शेष ‘remainder’ used as an adjective: ‘the remaining ones’. With दैत्याः (12.34): the Daityas who survived.

mantras.anvaya: (देव्या युधि देवरिपौ शुम्भे निहते —) जगद्विध्वंसिनि महोग्रे अतुलविक्रमे तस्मिन् (निहते), महावीर्ये निशुम्भे च (निहते), शेषाः (दैत्याः) पातालम् आययुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The locative absolutes begun in 12.34 continue: तस्मिन् resumes Śumbha with three epithets, and निशुम्भे च adds his brother (निहते is understood). The main clause is शेषाः (दैत्याः) पातालम् आययुः.
mantras.lit: — that destroyer of the world, very fierce, of matchless valour — and Niśumbha of great might (being slain), the remaining (Daityas) went to Pātāla.
mantras.tr: he, the world’s destroyer, fierce beyond measure and matchless in valour, and mighty Niśumbha too, the Daityas who were left went down to Pātāla.
mantras.tr_note: The English keeps the locative absolutes as one clause, ‘when Śumbha … had been slain (12.34) … he … and mighty Niśumbha too’. The order of deaths in the story (Niśumbha in chapter 9, Śumbha in chapter 10) is not the order of the verse.

comm.t: The surviving demons are not destroyed: they go to Pātāla, the netherworld. This is the alternative the Devī offered them before the battle, in the message carried by Śiva (8.26): ‘go to Pātāla, if you wish to live’. With 12.34 the terms of that message are carried out in full.
That the remnant survives in Pātāla is read as why the Goddess must come again (12.36; 11.54–55): adharma is driven back, not abolished.

mantras.anvaya_en: One sentence: subject with epithets, a concessive (नित्या अपि), the manner (पुनः पुनः सम्भूय), and verb with object.
mantras.lit: Thus that Blessed Goddess, though eternal, coming into being again and again, O king, carries out the protection of the world.
mantras.tr: In this way, O king, the Blessed Goddess, though she is eternal, comes forth again and again to protect the world.
mantras.tr_note: The absolutive सम्भूय and the finite verb कुरुते are rendered as ‘comes forth … to protect’.

comm.t: Medhas turns from the story to King Suratha (भूप) and states its lesson. It answers the paradox he set out at the beginning: she is eternal (नित्यैव सा, 1.64), yet is said to arise (सा नित्याप्यभिधीयते, 1.66). The same words return here: नित्या अपि … सम्भूय.

The verse joins the three caritas into one pattern: each time the world is threatened she appears, acts and withdraws — the pattern the Devī herself promised in 11.54–55 (‘whenever trouble born of the demons arises, then I shall descend’).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has Nityā as a name (name 136, नित्या). The two texts share the idea of a Goddess who is eternal and still manifests.

sandhi_exceptions.reason: Final ā before initial ṛ is left unjoined. Pāṇini allows a vowel before ṛ to stand without sandhi (optionally, there with shortening); the Purāṇic verse keeps the long ā. The metre requires the hiatus: तुष्टा ऋद्धिं प्रयच्छति has the eight syllables of the pāda, while the guṇa form तुष्टर्द्धिं would leave seven. The Gita Press prints the words apart.

morph.note: Passive of the causative मोहयति ‘causes to be bewildered’: the causative -अय- is dropped before the passive -य-: मोह्-य-ते. ‘Is made deluded (by her)’. Compare 1.55, तया सम्मोह्यते जगत्.

From the divādi root सू ‘to bring forth’, which is ātmanepada (सूयते): an active verb with विश्वम् as object. Read as the passive of the adādi root (सूते, passive सूयते) it would mean ‘is born’, which does not fit the nominative सा with the accusative विश्वम्.

√याच् takes two objects (‘to ask someone for something’); in the passive participle the person asked becomes the subject (सा याचिता, ‘she, being asked’), and विज्ञानम् may be taken either as the thing asked for or as the object of प्रयच्छति. Either way she gives knowledge when asked.

mantras.anvaya: तया एतत् विश्वं मोह्यते; सा एव विश्वं प्रसूयते। सा च याचिता विज्ञानं (प्रयच्छति), तुष्टा ऋद्धिं प्रयच्छति।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two balanced pairs: a passive and an active sentence about the universe (deluded by her, brought forth by her), and two participles of condition (याचिता, तुष्टा) each with its gift, sharing the verb प्रयच्छति.
mantras.lit: By her this universe is deluded; she herself brings forth the universe. And she, when entreated, (grants) knowledge; (when) pleased, she grants prosperity.
mantras.tr: By her this universe is held in delusion, and she herself gives birth to it. Entreated, she grants knowledge; pleased, she grants prosperity.

comm.t: Medhas gathers the Goddess’s powers in four clauses: she deludes the world, she brings it forth, she gives knowledge when asked, and prosperity when pleased. The same power that binds (मोह्यते) also releases (विज्ञानम्).

The verse repeats Medhas’s first teaching in chapter 1: Mahāmāyā deludes the world (तया सम्मोह्यते जगत्, 1.55), by her the universe is emitted (तया विसृज्यते विश्वम्, 1.56), and when gracious she becomes the cause of liberation (1.57). The story has been told between the two statements.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names her as the one who deludes and the one who gives birth to the world: मोहिनी (name 562) and वियदादिजगत्प्रसूः, ‘mother of the world beginning with space’ (name 550). The parallel is of idea, not of text.

mantras.anvaya: मनुजेश्वर, एतत् सकलं ब्रह्माण्डं महाकाले महामारीस्वरूपया तया महाकाल्या व्याप्तम् (अस्ति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A passive participial sentence: subject (ब्रह्माण्डम्), predicate (व्याप्तम्), agent तया expanded by महाकाल्या and its epithet; महाकाले gives the time.
mantras.lit: Pervaded by her is this entire cosmic egg, O lord of men — by Mahākālī, who at the great time (of dissolution) has the great Death (Mahāmārī) as her own form.
mantras.tr: O lord of men, this whole universe is pervaded by her — by Mahākālī, who at the great time of dissolution takes the form of Mahāmārī, the great destroyer.
mantras.tr_note: महाकाले is taken with महामारीस्वरूपया (‘at the great time, having the form of …’); it could also go with व्याप्तम् (‘at the great time the universe is pervaded by her’).

comm.t: Medhas, addressing Suratha (मनुजेश्वर), names the Goddess in her destroying aspect: Mahākālī, who at the ‘great time’ is Mahāmārī, the great Death that ends the world. In 12.8 the same word महामारी names the epidemics from which the text protects; here it is the cosmic power itself.

In the Gita Press pāṭha Mahākālī is also the presiding deity of the first carita (the liturgical viniyoga). Here the name is used in its own sense: the Goddess as Time’s destroying power at the dissolution.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also has the name Mahākālī (name 751, महाकाली). The texts remain distinct; the name is shared.

Feminine of सनातन ‘everlasting’ (from सना ‘always’). The same word addresses her in the gods’ hymn, सृष्टिस्थितिविनाशानां शक्तिभूते सनातनि (11.11).

mantras.anvaya: सा एव काले महामारी (भवति); सा एव अजा सृष्टिः भवति; सा एव सनातनी काले भूतानां स्थितिं करोति।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three clauses each opened by सा एव: dissolution, creation, preservation. भवति is understood in the first.
mantras.lit: She herself at (its) time is the great Death; she herself, the unborn, becomes creation; she herself, the eternal, in time makes the continuance of beings.
mantras.tr: She alone, when the time comes, is Mahāmārī, the great destroyer; she, the unborn, becomes creation; she, the eternal, sustains all beings in their time.

comm.t: The three works of the Goddess, each introduced by सा एव, ‘she alone’: dissolution (महामारी), creation (सृष्टिः) and preservation (स्थितिः). The list begins with destruction, continuing from 12.38. The epithets underline the paradox: the unborn (अजा) becomes creation; the eternal (सनातनी) acts in time (काले).

The gods’ hymn named her the power (शक्ति) of creation, preservation and destruction (11.11), and Brahmā’s hymn said she is creation in emission and preservation in sustaining (1.76). Here Medhas states the same as plain doctrine to Suratha.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the same three functions: सृष्टिकर्त्री (name 264), गोप्त्री (name 266) and संहारिणी (name 268); it also has अजा (name 866). The shared triad is common Śākta doctrine, stated in two separate works.

mantras.lit: In a time of prosperity she herself is Lakṣmī in the home of men, giving increase; she herself likewise, in (a time of) decline, arises as Alakṣmī for (their) ruin.
mantras.tr: In good times she is Lakṣmī in people’s homes, bringing increase; in times of decline she herself arises as Alakṣmī, bringing ruin.

comm.t: Fortune and misfortune are both her forms. The two lines mirror each other word by word: the time of flourishing and the time of want, Lakṣmī and Alakṣmī, increase and ruin.

The gods’ hymn in chapter 4 had said the same: she is Śrī herself in the homes of the virtuous and Alakṣmī in the homes of the wicked (या श्रीः स्वयं सुकृतिनां भवनेष्वलक्ष्मीः पापात्मनाम्, 4.5). There the difference is the householder’s conduct; here it is the season of fortune.
A modern reading: the verse refuses to divide the world into a good power and a hostile one. Gain and loss come from the same source; what changes is the time.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two participles of condition (स्तुता, सम्पूजिता) with instruments of worship, then the verb ददाति with four objects.
mantras.lit: Praised, and worshipped with flowers and likewise with incense, perfume and the rest, she gives wealth and sons, a mind (set) on dharma, and an auspicious course.
mantras.tr: Praised and worshipped with flowers, incense, perfume and the like, she gives wealth and children, a mind set on dharma, and a blessed destiny.
mantras.tr_note: पुत्रान्, ‘sons’, is rendered ‘children’; गतिं शुभाम्, literally ‘an auspicious going’, is rendered ‘a blessed destiny’ (the state one reaches, in this life or after it).

comm.t: The chapter of the fruits of recitation ends with a list of gifts that rises in order: wealth, children, a mind turned to dharma, and a good destiny. Praise (स्तुता) and worship (सम्पूजिता) are named together, as hymn and offering were in 12.20–24.

The closing ॐ (bīja) printed after this mantra belongs to the Gita Press pāṭha, not to the Purāṇa. The next chapter repeats the promise in Medhas’s last counsel to Suratha: worshipped, she grants enjoyment, heaven and final release (13.5).
A modern reading: the list does not stop at possessions. The last two gifts — a mind inclined to what is right, and a good end — are the ones no one can take away.
